To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) participants preferred tree representations for visualising hierarchical structure of organizations, but did not prefer trees for visualising arithmetic hierarchies, 2) trees were the most accurate, but parentheses took the most time in comprehension of hierarchical structure, 3) the results were less clear for trees and indentation.

(1) the naturalness of correspondence between a hierarchy and a tree is a strong predictor of the preference of a tree representation in production and comprehension; (2) the conventional usage of tree, indentation, and parentheses in the three application domains is a weak predictor of preference; and (3) in comprehension, the conventional usage of a diagrammatic representation in an application domain is a strong predictor for response time and accuracy.

(i) the natural correspondence between hierarchies in a given domain and a given diagrammatic representation is a strong determinant for the use of the representation in the production of hierarchies and (ii) the use of the same diagrammatic representation in a different domain may lead to performance losses.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of natural correspondence and convention, and the results indicate that the effects of convention are more important than those of natural correspondence in producing hierarchies.
the question whether the use of diagrams in a specific domain is based on a convention or on a natural correspondence between the domain and the diagram.
the question how to design effective diagrammatic interfaces for visualizing hierarchically ordered data.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the choice of representation is domain dependent.
the choice of representation should be domain-dependent.
there is no single diagrammatic representation that is best suited to all domains.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the results show that the choice of diagrammatic representation is not only determined by the inherent natural correspondence between the diagram and the information to be represented, but also by convention and the domain of application.
trees are preferred for visualizing and understanding hierarchical structure in general.
the use of a tree diagram for a hierarchy is not only natural, but also effective for comprehension.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the choice of diagram for visualizing hierarchies should be carefully considered, as it can affect the way users interact with the information.
there is a need to study the effect of domain knowledge and conventions on the use of diagrammatic representations in the design of interfaces.
the use of trees for representing hierarchical structure is not universal, and that the conventional representation for a given domain should be used.
